edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Diem Baptismo solemniorem Pascha praestat, cum et passio Domini in qua tinguimur, adimpleta est, nec incongruenter ad figuram interpretabitur, quod cum ultimum Pascha Dominus esset acturus, missis discipulis ad praeparandum, Invenietis, inquit, hominem aquam bajulantem Paschae celebrandae locum de signo aquae ostendit. Exinde Pentecoste ordinandis lavacris latissimum spatium est, quo et Domini resurrectio inter discipulos frequentata est, et gratia Spiritus sancti dedicata, et spes adventus Domini subostensa, quod tunc in coelos recuperato eo, Angeli ad apostolos dixerunt, sic venturum quemadmodum et in coelos conscendit utique in Pentecoste. Sed enim Jeremias cum dicit: Et congregabo illos ab extremis terrae in die festo, Paschae diem significat et Pentecostes, qui est proprie dies festus. Caeterum omnis dies Domini est, omnis hora, omne tempus habile Baptismo: si de solemnitate interest, de gratia nihil refert.
pass_a_gloss: The day of Baptism is more solemn than the Passover, since also the passion of the Lord in which we are baptized has been fulfilled, and it will not be interpreted incongruently with regard to the figure, because when the Lord was about to perform the last Passover, having sent the disciples to prepare, He says, You will find a man carrying water, the place of celebrating the Passover is shown by the sign of water. From then on, there is a very wide space for arranging the washings of Pentecost, in which also the resurrection of the Lord was frequented among the disciples, and the grace of the Holy Spirit was dedicated, and the hope of the coming of the Lord was hinted at, because then, when He had been taken back up into heaven, the Angels said to the Apostles, He will come in the same way as He ascended into heaven, certainly on Pentecost. But indeed Jeremiah, when he says, And I will gather them from the ends of the earth on a feast day, signifies the day of the Passover and of Pentecost, which is properly the feast day. Nevertheless, every day is the Lord's day, every hour, every time is suitable for Baptism: if it concerns solemnity, it does not matter concerning grace.
pass_b_english: Easter outranks Passover as the day for baptism, because the Lord's passion -- the very death we are plunged into -- has been accomplished, and the typology fits without strain: when Jesus was about to eat his final Passover, he sent the disciples ahead with the sign, "You will find a man carrying a water jar," and that water pointed to the place where the feast would be kept (Mark 14:13-15; Luke 22:10-12).

From that moment Pentecost opens a broad field for scheduling baptisms, since the risen Lord appeared repeatedly to his disciples then, the Holy Spirit's grace was poured out, and the hope of his return was signaled when the angels told the apostles, "He will come back in the same way you saw him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11) -- a promise stamped with Pentecost's own date.
Jeremiah clinches the double reference: "I will gather them from the ends of the earth on a feast day" (Jeremiah 31:8), naming both Passover and Pentecost, the latter being the feast day proper.
Even so, every day belongs to the Lord, every hour, every moment is fit for baptism; if the only difference is solemnity, grace itself makes no distinction.
